utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. May we hear the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Lise-Lotte Karlsson for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. John Ostojic on behalf of Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that we can start immediately with today's one and only witness, number 45. And if I recall correctly, you stated that no protective measures would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. The Defence does have a request of the Court, if we may, or we can apply for it at the end of his testimony. It involves three specific issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should try to resolve all the remaining issues after we have heard the witness, also from the side of the Judges, there are some issues to be discussed. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher, please, to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kos. Can you hear in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are now here as a witness of the Court. You are called by the Defence, and therefore the first line of questions will come from the side of the Defence. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my name is John Ostojic, and I represent Dr. Stakic, as you know. I'll be asking you a series of questions today, this morning, in connection with items and facts which you observed and those that were known to you in the spring and summer of 1992. If at any time you do not understand my question, please ask me to clarify the question, and I will attempt to do so. Let us begin. Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: My name is Mico Kos. I was born on the 6th of September, in 1952 in Lamovita, Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us your father's name, please.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Dragoljub.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Omladinski Put, 51 Street, Prijedor town, Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, sir, share with us your marital status.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I'm married, father of two daughters, one of them is a student and the other is an elementary school pupil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking, but can you share with us your ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of 1992, where did you reside?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: In Prijedor, the same address that I've just provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you lived at that address, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: For 20 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, your educational background. What is the highest level of education that you attained?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The highest level of education is completion of a university degree. I graduated from the economics faculty in Sarajevo in 1976. And I have been filling official -- high official positions ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us a little background of your employment history, sir, if you can, starting with where you were employed in the spring and summer of 1992 and in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: In 1992, or more specifically, ever since 1987, I have been manager of the Sana catering facility in the Prijedor Hotel in Prijedor. And then through to mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that in the spring and summer of 1992, you were the manager or director of the Hotel Prijedor in the very city of Prijedor, Prijedor Municipality? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's correct. The hotel is on the right bank of the River Sana.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, we can have the usher show the witness Exhibit S2, please. Perhaps S2-1 would also be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We would prefer S2-1, and focus, please, on the centre of the town and immediately on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, you have a map that has been provided as an exhibit and admitted into evidence. I'm going to ask you, please, to look at this map and share with us, if you can, where the hotel is in which you were the director in the spring and summer of 1992. There's a pointer on the desk in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Prijedor Hotel. This dark patch here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can ask -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please fix it. That's the building close to the -- is it a bridge? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask the witness to point again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, would you be kind enough to again show us where the Hotel Prijedor is.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Here, on the corner of -- I mean, the Sana River bank. And this street leading from the direction of Tukovi towards Ljubija and Sanski Most entering the town. Not the light part here, but the darker patch, the dark spot here. And it says clearly, it's marked "Hotel Prijedor." It has the letter P to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just leave the map there, and we'll come back to it in are a minute. I have some other preliminary questions. Mr. Kos, can you tell me prior to April of 1992, were you affiliated with any political party at any time?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the communist league of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you share with us the period of time in which you were a member of the communist league of Yugoslavia roughly, to the extent that you can recall.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I became a member when I was doing my regular military service in the JNA. That was back in 1977. And then I stayed in the party until late in 1993. But as soon as war broke out, there were no more party meetings being held. So until the war broke out, you could say I was effectively a member of the communist league.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period 1991 through 1993, were you, sir, at all a member of the political party the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I never was. I was, so to speak, neutral during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately prior to April of 1992, namely, January through April of 1992, did you have an opportunity to travel through the town of Prijedor for both personal and employment reasons?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Prijedor every day at that time. I would go to work. I would pass through the centre of the town, and I often took my wife out to the centre in the evening to do some shopping, to walk around a bit, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will not need the map for another few moments, so not to inconvenience the usher, if we can remove the map and then we'll come back to it, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, I'd like to ask you things which you observed during that time period of approximately January through April of 1992. And specifically, before we address that issue, share with us what your duties and obligations were as the director of the Hotel Prijedor at that time frame.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, my duties and responsibilities as the manager were to organise the work of the company from the top level down, down to security issues and representation of the hotel to clients, to external clients, and to the hotel's caterers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say clients and hotel's caterers, you actually mean guests of the hotel. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you share with us from the period January through April 1992 whether or not Hotel Prijedor under your direction and management had employees who were of diverse ethnic backgrounds, meaning were there Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and otherwise as we have called here other non-Serbs who were employed at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Throughout that period, all the employees, until the 31st of December, 1991, stayed in their positions, and they kept on working, business as usual, true enough. There was less work to be dealt with at that time. We had the least number of Croats, but Serbs and Muslims were equally represented in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm only focussing for my purposes now the period prior to the 30th of April, 1992, if I can. So that period, there were both Serbs and Bosniak Muslims, predominantly, at the hotel, correct, as employees? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, let me ask you, were you able to observe or did you learn first-hand from your employees that people, families, were leaving the Prijedor Municipality because of tensions or the atmosphere of fear that was starting to develop in the municipality? Again, sir, I'm only asking you for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: As I told you at the beginning, I spent quite some time in the centre. And you did feel a certain atmosphere, the migration of the population, the bus terminal was often full of people as well as the railway station. Usually there were bussing running from Prijedor to other places, and those buses were always packed. It was difficult to get a ticket if you were going to Zagreb or Belgrade or any place like that. A case I can remember right now, a waiter who used to work at the hotel asked for unpaid leave. And he told me openly that he had sent his wife and children away out of Bosnia to a safer place, he said. I granted his leave, and at a later stage he reported back to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here, do you recall that gentleman's name?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I do, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share it with us, please.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: His name was -- he was the chief waiter, Senad Kurtovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I think he's a Muslim. Mind you, I never drew up any lists with people's ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to observing people leaving or having the buses, I should say, full, did you also have an opportunity to discuss or did you learn from Mr. Mujadzic whether he had his family leave the Prijedor Municipality during this time period January through April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally present and talked to Mr. Mujadzic at the hotel once. And there were other people, there, too. And he said it himself, I sent my wife and two sons away to the Federal Republic of Germany. I think he said it back in March sometime. But it was spring 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, to the best of your recollection, whether that was a voluntarily exodus by his family, or was it involuntary, forced?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I think it was perfectly voluntary. There was no coercion, no use of force, by anyone there, any of the different ethnic groups, I think, at least not that I noticed any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, did you notice, sir, while the buses were filled with people that were departing the Prijedor Municipality, did you notice any coercion or forced exodus or transfer of these people?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no coercion whatsoever. I knew of Serbs leaving, migrations, on a day-to-day basis. They would send their children away. Most usually people were sending their wives and children away. People there knew from experience that there had been the war in Croatia in 1991, so many people became afraid and they wanted to save the lives of their closest kin. There was nothing organised about it in that period; life went on as normal. Work went on as normal. The economy, the political life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if I may, during that period of time, was there an influx in the Prijedor Municipality of people who were coming from Croatia as a result of the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a certain influx, but I wouldn't exactly call it significant. Plenty of our own people who worked in Zagreb and Ljubija in Croatia and in Slovenia came back, but not too many, I would say. They were running from the war in Slovenia and Croatia so they returned to their homes so to speak, because that was very often where their parents lived, their brothers and sisters perhaps. So they had their own place to stay when they came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, sir, now, to the period of April 30th, 1992, if you can just briefly identify for me if you know what the significance, if any, of that date is.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The 30th of April is usually taken as the date of the takeover by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me also ask you for purposes of a time line, are you familiar or did you become familiar with the date of May 22nd, 1992? Did something happen that may be considered significant on that date?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I remember that date. You said the 22nd of May, and that's correct. There was an incident near -- just below Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I just want to establish that you are familiar with those time lines, and then I'm going to ask you some questions of things that you may have personally observed and experienced within that time line. We'll get to the 22nd of May and that which you learned and observed personally. Right now, I'm concentrating, with the Court's permission, on that specific approximate three-week period. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From April 30th, 1992, through May 22nd, 1992, did Muslims, Croatians, and other non-Serbs continue to be gainfully employed at the Hotel Prijedor in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes. It was business as usual for everyone. The first day, things started happening, and the next 20 days, they reported for work. There was a certain amount of fear in the air. People were saying things. People were asking me for advice. And whenever I was approached, I would always tell them "I don't think you'll be running into any problems. Everything goes on as usual." So people came to work. And I wouldn't say that tensions were particularly high or that fear was extreme. There was a certain amount of fear with the non-Serb population, but everyone turned up for work regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, in your capacity as the director of the Hotel Prijedor have the ability to discharge and fire employees who worked under you at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I was not in a position. I was not legally authorised to do that. My employees came to work on a regular basis. I had no desire, intention, or plans to fire anyone regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you that in a moment. My question to you, sir, is whether you could have been able to, during that time period, the 30th of April through May 22nd, 1992, fire or dismiss an employee who may have been derelict in his duties in any way? Were you the man who would discharge them?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to. But there was the labour law. I was there to apply it, but I had no other instructions, no instructions other than that, from any of the official structures to fire non-Serbs from work, no matter which point in time we're speaking about. People did get sick occasionally, and they would give us a ring to tell them they were on sick leave. Obviously such cases were tolerated, but there were no repercussions in such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may ask you directly, did you during this time period discharge, dismiss, or fire any employees who were of an ethnic background different than yours, namely, Muslims, Croats, or other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Once, not once, I never fired a single employee at my hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, during that time period at any time harass or intimidate any of your non-Serb employees?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I believe that I didn't. There were never any complaints to that effect. We had a system of internal monitoring whereby employees could complain about their manager's behaviour. But no complaints were ever filed against me, not in my company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We briefly discussed the date of May 22nd, 1992. I'm not going to ask you to tell us what you heard about necessarily the incident, the number of the military men who were attacked and killed, but I'd like to have you share with us whether or not you were at the hotel on May 22nd, 1992, when you heard about the incident at Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: This event took place in the evening hours, while I was at home. I got a phone call from the chief waiter who wanted to inform me. It must have been around 22, 23 hours, to inform me that he couldn't, since he lived in Ljubija, 12 kilometres from Prijedor, that he couldn't go through Hambarine, that the buses were not driving, that there was a crowd of people, that something had happened. And he wanted me to give him my approval to stay there, to spend the night there, which is what I did. And it was on the next morning that we heard what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here, sir, do you recall the ethnic background of this employee who asked you for permission to stay overnight at the hotel as a result of the incident on May 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Anusic, nicknamed Nono, who was the chief waiter at the hotel, a Croat by ethnicity. And his friend Misa and myself, we celebrated Christmas together in 1991. He was a good friend of mine, like many other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These other friends of yours, were they also, sir, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Like I just told you, one was a Muslim, one was a Croat, and one was a Serb, and we celebrated the Catholic Christmas together in 1991. Mr. Kosar [as interpreted] who is now living in Rijeka can confirm that. Misa was also there, but I'm not sure where he is at the moment, whether he's in Europe or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another time line, sir, we had established I believe in this case is the date of May 24th, 1992, which was an incident that occurred at Kozarac, and I'm sharing, with the Court's permission, just some background on this. I'm taking you through the period of May 24th, 1992, through May 30th, 1992. But before I ask you a series of questions for that time period, I would like to know if you know the significance of the date of May 30th, 1992. What if anything occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we previously stipulated to that date during one of the cross-examinations a long time -- I remember it was Mr. Lukic who was asking the witness that question. But just to shorten things, all these dates, the takeover, the 30th of April, the Hambarine incident, the 22nd of May, the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, the Prosecution offers to stipulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but for purposes of credibility of the witness, I think it's important to know, and the Defence's position is if we examine those incidents and those dates, it would assist us when comparing the fourth amended indictment as to truly what transpired. If this witness had no knowledge of that time period, the Court would weigh, perhaps, his testimony slightly differently and if he did have knowledge of it, the Defence has specific questions, and I can share with the Court what it is, of movement of people from the Kozara area in the city of Prijedor itself where he was the director of the hotel. So we would like to establish that fact, and it's necessary for us in order that it's not vague or broad that specifically within that time period, Mr. Kos was the hotel director; specifically within that time period, he personally observed that families from the Kozara area were seeking shelter and came to the city of Prijedor. And then hopefully there's going to be an explanation as to what some of these people did who resided within the city of Prijedor on or about May 30th, 1992. I think we have a right to establish that. We're not disputing the dates. In fact, it was the Defence who insisted that these dates be clarified. If the Court examines the fourth amended indictment, the 22nd of May, 1992, although enormously significant as stipulated to is not mentioned by the OTP. The 24th of May, 1992, a very significant date is not mentioned. How the provocation occurred, all they do is mention a period of May through June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, no argument. We are not with the closing argument now. And we have not the slightest doubt as to the credibility of the witness as he sits here. And therefore, this should be not disputed. It's not necessary to establish. And since we received the fourth amended indictment, we have heard now 93 days of testimony, all in all, more than 9.000 pages. And I think even though the parties unfortunately did not succeed to come to agreed facts, these facts seem to be -- we have to be cautious -- seem to be undisputed. And therefore, it seems to be absolutely not necessary. And I think it's also established that all people living in Prijedor at that time are aware of these important days, be it the 30th of April, be it the 22nd of May. So therefore, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just trying to avoid an objection on foundation, so I was trying to establish that the witness is aware of those time lines. So if I may, I will proceed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, from the 24th of May, 1992, through the 30th of May, 1992, did you have an opportunity on a continuous and daily basis go to the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I only went to work during that time period because the tension after all had mounted. But I went to work normally, and I went back home normally. But it is true that not many people really walked around a lot or ventured out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: -- shopping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. During that time period, sir, May 24th through the 30th of May, 1992, did you personally observe and learn that people from the area identified as Kozarac were coming into the town to live with family, friends, and, in fact, also stayed at your hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember one particular night when a large group of people had arrived. I don't remember exactly the gentleman who was the leader of the group and who wanted the accommodation for only one night, which is what I accepted. We never charged them for that. They spent the night there and then left the next day. I don't remember the exact date, but you can find it in the records of the hotel. But I know it was during that time period after the 24th, when a large group of people arrived to stay with their relatives and those who couldn't find accommodation with their relatives, they came to the hotel. And we organised the accommodation for them. It is possible that some of them stayed two nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kos. Specifically, now, I would like to ask you about the 30th of May, 1992. Although stipulated, can you tell us, if you recall, on that date what you remember occurred.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I do recall that day very well. I'll never forget it. I was fortunate to have survived, although it was my baptism in fire. It was a Saturday. And I went to work and ran into an ambush. I don't know what to call it. It was some sort of clash between the extremists who had come to Prijedor town to recapture it. I don't know if you want to hear the details. Anyway, I got to the JNA Street, which is leading to the hotel, and I got to the street in front of the hotel which is called Partizanska Street. And as I was getting closer to the hotel, I could hear shooting. I heard it from my car, and I could even sense that there was something bumping against my car. I crossed the street. I got to the junction. And when I was about to leave -- to turn left towards the hotel, I saw fire and smoke near the hotel. It was 7.00 in the morning, and it was drizzling. And at that point, I heard really loud shooting. I turned right towards the orthodox church and went in the direction of Jereza, which is a local commune there. I didn't have any problems at that point as I was driving, and I thought perhaps I should go back to JNA street where I had come from. But I turned right nevertheless towards the Jereza neighbourhood, and I heard -- I realised that my car was being shot at with a burst of gunfire. I fell down, and I was then closer to the hotel. This was now the right side of the hotel. And I was really exposed to the fire. There was a civilian car there, a Zastava 101 car, and I saw that it had crashed against a lamppost, and there was a man lying next to the car. And when I looked up, I realised that the shooting was coming from the park. There was this person, as I said, lying down, a body of a citizen lying next to the car. I couldn't see what was inside the car. But at any rate, it had crashed against the lamppost with the front part. I continued driving my car. I ducked, but I could still see a little. I was able to follow the road, and then I passed by the local museum of Prijedor. And I saw that there was a truck parked there. I glanced in the direction of Suporek, and I thought that I might be safer there, but I realised that there were some people in uniform there in vicinity of the museum. They were facing the SUP building and pointing their rifles towards the SUP building. I turned a bit to the right with my car and passed by this group of people and this truck without problems at that point. But when I reached the crossing of Karadzic Street and Vojvoda Put Street, I saw a delivery truck that was delivering bread to the local shops. There was another group of people consisting of two or three soldiers maybe. One of whom was standing next to this vehicle, and I passed by this vehicle on the left side. I couldn't tell that bullets were being fired at me. They were probably surprised. They didn't expect anyone coming their way. And the first thing that occurred to me that I should do -- I reversed into neutral, and I continued towards another junction there where I left the car, and I ran out of the car and ran towards my home. This took place between 7.15, at around 7.15 or 7.20. I don't know if this means anything to you. Two or three days later, I fetched the car. But I was able to -- I was able to count 20 or 30 bullets later on when I fetched the car. I was lucky because one of the bullets hit the filter. One hit the carburetor. So -- well, I was really lucky. This was just my personal experience. As I said, it was a Saturday and since the hotel is after all a catering facility, I also worked on Saturday, and I had normally gone to work that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Permit me to ask you a couple questions if I may in connection to that, sir. You identified initially that this group that were attacking the town were extremists. Can you identify for me, sir, how is it first of all that you know that this group were extremists?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Who else but extremists if it was by force that they wanted to impose their version of justice with weapons?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this group, sir, resisting anything, or were they attacking the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: They were attacking. They were trying to capture the city of Prijedor from several directions. This is what I learned later. My people in the hotel who had spent the night at the hotel told me about it. A man got killed, and this driver, the Zitopromet driver, was also killed, the civilian who was driving this truck. One of the groups was attacking the Prijedor Hotel. There was a bakery shop which we called Kanape, a privately owned bakery shop located in the street leading to Tukovi. And this is where they came from, this group of extremists, who were attacking the hotel. When I finally got home on that day, around 12.00, I wasn't -- in those days, I didn't listen to the Prijedor radio, but the Zagreb radio. And I heard that the hotel had been captured, that it was on fire and so on and so forth. I didn't believe everything that I heard, of course, and then in the afternoon I heard that the hotel had not actually been captured by the extremists. One other group was at the local secondary school. They were also firing towards the Prijedor Hotel. I think that that was the strongest group of all. I have a couple of friends who told me they had been captured. One of them passed away in the meantime. One was a bank clerk, Brane, then Marijan Nisic. There was quite a few of them, but I know these two men who were captured while going to work wearing civilian clothes like myself. They were taken prisoners by them and detained in a classroom of the secondary technical school. They interrogated them there. I don't know whether they had tied them up or not, whether they had been tortured or not. But...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, let me just ask a couple questions still with respect to the 30th of May and this attack by extremists. Did you learn and come to know what the ethnic background of these extremists who attacked the city of Prijedor on May 30th, 1992, was?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: What I learned later and what I'm sure about, they were Muslims and Croats. I was very good friends with Slavko Ecim actually, and he was one of them who had organised the whole thing. He was pretty outspoken. He had even spoken publicly about it. And he would say publicly that things would be different, that they would not turn out according to what Serbs had planned and so on and so forth. So there were quite of few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately the number of people that were involved in this attack, as you call it, by the extremists on the 30th of May, on the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, no one was able to establish that. I can only tell you how many checkpoints there were that were manned by these extremists. I told you about two of them. Then there was a third one where a large group of people was near the Kozarski Vjesnik office and the Prijedor radio. That's where one group went. And there was another one that came from the direction of the Balkan Hotel; that's four. The fifth one was at the overfly, the one that had come from Puharska. I think that it was the largest one actually according to what people said. A very good friend of mine was severely wounded there. A friend who was an ambulance driver. He was seriously ill later on. He had a heart attack. I don't know whether this was related with what had happened or not. But anyway, this group was able to control one of the access roads to Prijedor, the area which we call Prijedor 2 where some of the military and the police were located. So everyone who went underneath this overfly was shot dead. And that is what Dragovic told me. They were shooting from heavy weapons, and this was the -- the group that people feared most. And then the group that went -- that attacked the hotel and set it on fire, they were able to set on fire the area which consists of -- which was made of inflammable substance. I mean, the furniture there was made of inflammable substance. So there were quite a few such groups, one of them very well armed even with machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within those groups that you've mentioned, approximately how many people were in each group, sir, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I don't think I can say how many. I saw only a couple of people in front of the museum, and then groups of five or six people in front of the local grammar school. As for the other secondary school building near the park, that was further away, so I couldn't see. But this is where I heard the shooting was coming from, from the park near the secondary school. And they shot at my car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The extremists who attacked the town of Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992, were they shooting, sir, at the military -- or first, I should ask you, was there a military presence within that town? And if so, to what extent?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: There was almost no military inside the town. There were two checkpoints which they attacked. They attacked one near the Hotel Prijedor from the direction of Tukovi, and they killed one or two people there. I know that there was a checkpoint there which came under attack. It was manned by a mixed group consisting of both military and civilian police. There was no actual -- any military strictly speaking inside the town. There was a group, again, a mixed group, near the officers' club in the town, both civilian and military policemen. So that's all. The soldiers were not located inside the town. They were quartered further away, in the barracks, in the garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, share with us, if you know, from your personal observations, who were these as you call them extremists on the 30th of May, 1992, who attacked the city of Prijedor? Who were they attacking?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: They were attacking vital points inside the town such as the Radio Prijedor station which they wanted to take possession of, and the office of the local newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik, the town hall, that is the municipality building, in order to take over. They had attacked the official authorities of the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having lived in the Prijedor Municipality and working specifically in the city of Prijedor, were you, sir, able to make an assessment as to where these extremists were coming from who attacked the town on the 30th of May, 1992, from which direction or which part?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, I described the direction they had come from. A group came from the direction of Puharska and Cerek, and the other one from the area of Hambarine, the hilly part of the municipality. They must have crossed the Sana River. And one group came from the side. I don't know exactly which areas they had come from, Kozarac, Jakupovici, Cela, thereabouts. But I'm not sure. I don't know exactly from where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, exactly which area of the town these extremists who attacked the town of Prijedor retreated to?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I wasn't present, but I know according to what people told me one -- a friend of mine told me that the majority of them had withdrawn towards the area of Stari Grad, and then further on across the Sana River and the area of the Hambarine hill. The largest part of the extremists went in the direction of Stari Grad, and then they crossed the Sana River in boats and were withdrawing further on into the fields and the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see, sir, whether there was battles that were raging from house to house?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I was not. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time see or observe or come to the conclusion that there were snipers in town who were also attacking the city?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I noticed that there were snipers on that morning when I was driving to work. I noticed something strange, and I was later on told that those had been snipers because there is a difference between normal shooting and between -- and the shots which are fired from sniping rifles. And then there would be a lull in shooting, and then they would start again opening fire from these rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, you informed us of a conversation that you had with a gentleman by the name of Slavko Ecim in connection with him being one of the leaders of this extremist group who attacked the city of Prijedor. And you mentioned, I believe, that he was a good friend of yours, or a friend of yours. Can you tell us when that conversation happened between you and Mr. Ecim?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That was earlier. That was long before the attack. It may have been in 1991, I think. Afterwards, I didn't meet Ecim any more. We were friends, but through another friend that we shared, Vojo Topic. There's nothing secretive about it. He was a friend of mine. He was into private business before the war, so he constructed fish ponds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the attack on Prijedor, up until and including September 30th, 1992, can you describe for us what, if anything, was happening in the city of Prijedor, specifically as you personally observed it while you were gainfully employed at the Hotel Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, yes, a lot happened. You mean since the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 30th, through September of 1992, was there some normalcy that was attempting to be returned to the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, gradually, yes, life was back to normal and work was back to normal. You could feel that the economy had been affected, but it continued operating, although there were cutbacks everywhere. In the catering business, not to speak of the Celpak and the iron ore mines, the really big companies. They practically halved their production, because the roads were unsafe, and traffic was often impossible, and the supply of goods was cut off. But people did move about. The Mlado sports hall, there were buses there, and some people were leaving. I wasn't really interested. I wasn't there myself when these things were happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, tell us if you personally know Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And share with us how is it that you first met Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: First, I had heard of him. I heard that he was a doctor who was from Omarska. That's where he completed elementary school, and he worked there later on. He had finished med school, and then he came to Omarska to work. I got to know him a bit better. There was a promotional meeting for Veljko Guberina's party. Veljko Guberina is a lawyer from Belgrade. The name of the party is I think was the National Radical Party. That was in the village of Nisevici. And that's where my wife comes from. So I decided just to go and see my relatives there, and I saw that the meeting was taking place. So I stopped by to have a word with the people at that meeting. And Mr. Stakic was one of the prominent founding members of that party in the Omarska area. From that time to the time when he was appointed vice-president, I didn't see them. But then I sort of met him again when he was the vice-president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. That was I think in 1990, after the first democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also, sir, have an opportunity to know Mr. Cehajic, who was the president of the Municipal Assembly, prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, Cehajic. I had met him in my early days. I was working at a secondary school as an economics teacher, and Mr. Cehajic worked at the grammar school. He was teaching Serbo-Croatian. There was a restaurant nearby where we often had breakfast together, so I think I'm entitled to say that I knew him quite well, ever since 1979 when I returned from the army. I knew most of the grammar school teachers, especially the grammar teachers because that was the adjacent building to the building where I worked. So we had this restaurant that we often went to together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The period immediately prior to the 30th of April, 1992, did you have an opportunity to visit personally with Mr. Cehajic to sit and have a cup of coffee perhaps at your hotel or to visit with him in other places?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic really left a very favourable impression. He never passed by the Prijedor Hotel without seeing me, without having coffee with me. I mean, as a person, but when he became the president of the Municipal Assembly, he no longer came very often, but he did come once or twice. So we would exchange some remarks over a cup of coffee. So if there's anything that should be said about him, I think he was one of the more moderate people in our town and in our area. There was nothing extremist about him, and he never said anything against any of the ethnic groups. He always wanted peace. But I think I should say this: He once told me, Were it not for the hawks, for the extremists, we would be able to organise life in a much better way and turn Prijedor into perhaps the most beautiful place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because we did have opportunities to organise normal life, both in terms of the economy and in terms of the local politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn or become familiar with who these hawks or extremists were, sir? And if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no, not really. Other than what I've told you. Prior to that -- I'm not sure, so I don't want to be guessing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cehajic at any time criticise, complain, or render any negative opinions to you about Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, truth to tell, we never discussed this very much. He never said any bad things about Dr. Stakic, but he never said any particularly good things about him either. I certainly would remember if he had ever made any comments about him or if he had criticised him. I don't usually go around asking people, Well, what do you think about this man or about that man? I just know that in our conversations he never told me anything bad about him. He never called him an extremist. He never said that he was an impossible man to work with. He told me on the contrary that they worked well together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share with me, sir, with respect to Dr. Stakic if you heard him ever give a speech, a statement, or comment that would be in any fashion interpreted as being discriminatory against Muslims, Croats, or non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No. I never read anything in the printed media to that effect, not that I really read the local papers. And I don't listen to the radio much either. But in conversation, I never heard any open criticism of Dr. Stakic. I never heard anyone call him a hawk or an extremist. I never heard anyone say that he treated anyone from the SDA or the HDZ unfairly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all the questions we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution wants to start immediately, or should we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, yes, it's better to have the break now. The trial stays adjourned until 10.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, you may start, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the usher could move the ELMO to the side. If you could move it back, it's actually now right in his face. Cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned your good friend Slavko Ecim. Is Mr. Ecim also known as Slavko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Ecimovic, Ecimovic. Without an "H" at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ecimovic was a very educated and principled man, your friend. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: He was my friend's friend actually. I was more of an acquaintance really, not a close friend. We had a friend in common who was sort of the link between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you meet someone even for short time, you can tell the difference between an uncultured person and a person who is very cultured and displays an obvious dignity. And Mr. Ecimovic had that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, to quite a high extent I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, when Mr. Ecimovic told you prior to the events you talked about, prior to the Serb takeover of Prijedor, that things would not turn out as the Serbs had planned, he was very, very wrong, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's the way it turned out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about extremists and your definition, which I understand. And just to repeat it, you said that extremists would be someone who would have to be -- if by force, they wanted to impose their own version of justice, that these would be extremists. Sir, the people that took power on the 30th of April, 1992, were those people in your view extremists?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, I beg to differ on this, because the takeover happened without a single bullet being fired. No one got killed. No one was injured. So there's a difference between the use of force and a nonviolent takeover. So that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, why was the takeover successful without a bullet being fired? Why is it that people who had -- were elected and had positions such as the gentleman you mentioned, Mr. Cehajic, forced out of office so easily without a bullet being fired? Wasn't it -- I put it to you, sir, wasn't it because there was overwhelming force in favour of the side that was taking power?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: This is a political issue really. I wasn't moving in those circles exactly, so I don't think I can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked about the period after the takeover and said there was very little army presence. There were checkpoints, and there were guards stationed outside of key facilities such as the Municipal Assembly building following the takeover. Isn't that correct? Guards of some type, of some --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that most of these from -- do I understand you correctly that most of these were actually police, reserve police, and were not regular army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked in quite some detail about witnessing the attack on Prijedor. By the way, have you ever told any representatives of the Defence before today about your experiences during that attack and what you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Which period before are you referring to? Yes, I did talk to representatives of the Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. My question could be clearer. Let me try to start making clearer questions. When were you first approached by the Defence for Dr. Stakic about being a witness?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Perhaps a year ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. I think roughly a year ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Can you tell us who it was that first approached you and just briefly describe the contact you had.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the lawyer, approached me, Branko Lukic. He obtained certain information about me as a civilian in Prijedor having survived, because many people could have been killed or injured during the attack on Prijedor. So I took up his offer to tell my story the way I saw things, so that's why I took up the offer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We appreciate that, and we appreciate you coming. When you spoke to -- have you had other contacts or other interviews about your experiences in 1992 in Prijedor with the Defence besides this initial contact with Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spoke to Mr. Lukic a year ago, and that was the only contact you had prior to coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: We had other contacts. The first time and other two interviews, one was a kind of preparation, and then last Monday, just before I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During those interviews, did you tell the -- whoever it was you were speaking to, Mr. Lukic or whoever, about your experiences during the attack on Prijedor, on the 30th of May, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the hotel that you were the manager of -- I believe it's called the Prijedor Hotel. Correct? Hotel Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It sits more or less right on the banks of the Sana River, next to the bridge that connects the Tukovi neighbourhood to the main centre of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there was a checkpoint there that was guarding the entrance to the town?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Across -- from the hotel, you have a view also of Stari Grad. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: From the hotel, on the upper floors, yes. From the upper floors you do have a view of Stari Grad. There is a seafood restaurant there, and then there is the Berek, and then some sort of a canal and a restaurant. But Stari Grad, you can't really see Stari Grad from the ground floor of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I haven't had the pleasure of staying in your hotel yet. Can you tell us how many floors --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll have an opportunity, I hope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope so. How many storeys is your hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the restaurant -- you mentioned a restaurant. Is that on the top floor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No. The restaurant is on the first floor. And on the ground floor, you have the reception and some other hotel services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the -- you mentioned the upper storeys, it's possible to have a view of all of Stari Grad. Is that correct? It's simply the canal in between your hotel and Stari Grad. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. When you were witnessing the attack, were you staying on the ground floor? Were you outside the hotel or inside the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I was on my way to work. It was 7.00 in the morning. I was outside the hotel. I watched the hotel in flames, so I couldn't come any closer. So I turned back and went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you saw the attackers at one point crossing by boat, crossing the Sana River. That would be going from the side --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that. There must have been a translation error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have the transcript, so perhaps I didn't understand you. Did you say you saw that the attackers withdrawing to the fields and woods? And I thought you said they crossed the river.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: What I said was that I knew they were going in that direction. I didn't say that I saw them, but they were retreating through Stari Grad across the Sana River, to the fields, and then on to the forest. That's what eyewitnesses told me, but I didn't personally witness this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that would also make sense because if you were retreating and outnumbered, the woods would give cover to those persons who were trying to make an escape. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, approximately what time of day was that that this group of attackers withdrew across the river?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: According to the news I was listening to, and I was listening to Radio Zagreb, the hotel was not captured until 3.00 in the afternoon. So I assume they retreated from the centre after 3.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you re-enter the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Four days later, three or four days. That was the next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that -- how long did you stay in the area on the 30th -- and witness the attack on Stari Grad or the fighting in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: This lasted for about -- no, it wasn't in Stari Grad. It was in the town centre in general. 20 or 30 minutes, half an hour perhaps, as long as it took me to sort of circle that particular neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the fighting was not in Stari Grad, but closer to the centre around the hotel and on your side, the centre side of the river?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. I saw those fights. But later on, there were other fights before they crossed the River Sana. That's what I heard from eyewitness accounts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the individuals that you saw, that you actually saw, were armed with rifles of some sort. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to Stari Grad before and after that attack?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Before Stari Grad, Stari Grad was -- well, what should I say? But after the attack, there was a lot of destruction. Seven to ten days later perhaps; I can't quite remember the date when I ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't clear in my question. I meant during and after the attack. Did you see that there was the -- Stari Grad the day after the attack? The 31st of May, did you see Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. That was later, on Thursday or Friday the following week because for two or three days, I didn't go to the centre at all. I stayed at home with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that -- isn't it true that after that day, in the next couple days, people were told to go to your hotel, non-Serbs, where they were transported from there to camps such as Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stari Grad, I understand, means the "old town." And is it true that that was a somewhat unique section of Prijedor, that it had architecture and buildings from the Ottoman period, time?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, that's not my opinion. Stari Grad was surrounded, encircled, by a canal, which separates it from the rest of the town. It's a canal, and we refer to that neighbourhood as Stari Grad. There were old Bosnian houses, but not from the Ottoman period. That's far from the Ottoman empire, I would say. I could even tell you that in the former system, Stari Grad was supposed to be transformed into a recreation centre. And many of the houses had been bought off for that purpose, and their purpose was to become strictly tourism and cultural, tourism. That's what I knew. It was supposed to be a monument of culture, a certain number of houses. But then -- a number of houses had been bought off to be converted into a recreation -- into recreational and sports facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, these were houses that people were living in up until the 30th of May, 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was an almost completely Muslim neighbourhood. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a very -- there was a mosque there, an old mosque. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. On the island itself, a mosque, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you could see that mosque from your hotel. You could see the minaret of that mosque from your hotel. There was a mosque in Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The old mosque was in the centre of the town only. But I mean, I'm not sure. What I remember was it was located in the centre. If there was a mosque there, then, well, there must have been. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Stari Grad destroyed? How was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The day when the extremists were withdrawing, and then when the military arrived to chase them away, on that day. That's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it destroyed by tank fire, or were fires set? How was it destroyed? You don't destroy a house with a --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. A tank was used on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Stari Grad burning that day and the next few days?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not in the area for about four days, from that morning until Saturday, so I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I go to Stari Grad today, will I see it rebuilt, or will I still see the damaged buildings from the tank fire? What will I see if I go to Stari Grad today?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: You will not see damaged buildings; you will see an old house which is called Stari Loric, that has remained untouched, and a number of completely new houses that have been built in the meantime. And then an open area which was used as a flea market, but the population has moved out from the area, and new houses are being built.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt. Sorry. I think it's time now to ask you, Mr. Witness, Mr. Kos, to concentrate on the answers. This is not the place just to say this and that word. We want to have concrete and truthful answers. You have given a solemn declaration. And I will not tolerate that when asked you, for example, describe the way Stari Grad was destroyed, and then later on when asked, you tell just "I was not there." So please, tell us what you have seen yourself and refrain from speculations. And if you don't know, tell the representative of the Prosecution what you saw, what you did not see, what you maybe have heard from others. But don't leave this open in this way as if this would be just a conversation in your coffee shop of your hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what happened to the people that lived in Stari Grad after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your friend Slavko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask your brother what happened to Slavko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: My brother? No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother was a commander at the Omarska camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: He's not my brother. He's a cousin of mine, but a distant cousin of mine. His grandfather and my grandfather are brothers, and we are cousins three times removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. And just, for the record, can you say his first name, because I'll mispronounce it.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes. Milojica Kos, also known as Krle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your cousin, did you ever speak to him about the fate of Mr. Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I never talked to him about the Omarska camp at all, not even since he has come back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to him about the fate of Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned attending a -- running across some type of political rally for Mr. Guberina's party. That was in 1990. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Pre-electoral activities in 1989 or 1990, I'm not sure. The elections took place in 1990, so this could have been in 1989. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't immediately before the election, but sometime after the beginning of the multi-party system. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the platform of that radical party?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an educated resident of Prijedor, were you aware of the general view of political parties as far as their political views as far as which were considered -- for example, there were the reformists of Markovic, and then there were the nationalist parties. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was known that the reformists were more pro-Yugoslav, and the nationalist parties had advanced their own agendas. Correct? Anti-communists and their own nationalist agendas also. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the SDS party, was the radical party of Mr. Guberina seen as more nationalistic than the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Stakic, Dr. Stakic, when you met him, he was, your understanding, one of the founding members. Do you know that he was -- if he was actually -- that he was actually the first president of that party in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar, can you give us any insight, on how it was that Dr. Stakic became a member or became the SDS candidate for advice president of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, in order to stick to the caution given by His Honour, I only heard that the area of Omarska, within the structure of the government, wanted one office. And that office was the office of the vice-president of the municipality. And that is how they probably ended up with the -- with an adequate individual. I know that this distribution is done at the local level, for local communes, and the relevant areas, Ljubija, Omarska. Those were the former municipalities which were made part of the Prijedor Municipality, and he they probably requested each one office in one relatively important office within the local government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we do appreciate you making the distinction between things you know from your own observations and those you heard. That's important. Thank you. You talked about -- You talked about - in answer to one of Mr. Ostojic's questions - that you hadn't heard Dr. Stakic make any remarks that you thought were extremist or discriminatory against non-Serbs. Did you hear Dr. Stakic, when he was the president of the municipality, in the media, did you hear him on the radio, television, or in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you answered that question about not hearing him make any discriminatory remarks, what you meant is that you didn't hear him make any speeches at all. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I never heard or read anything about him. As I said, when I have time to read, I read the Belgrade-based Politika, and I watch the Zagreb TV. These are the sources of information that I mostly use. I don't listen to any local news agencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- thank you for telling us that. But do you recall when it was that Dr. Stakic returned to Prijedor and, once again, became the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it was 1995 or 1996 or somewhere in that time period?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that put Dr. Stakic forward as the president of the municipality, or how it was that he came back to once again become the president of the Serb municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I know that human resources policy was not conducted by the party that was in power, the SDS. I never attended any meetings or sessions of the close circles of the SDS leadership. I don't know the exact answer. But I assume it was them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Dr. Stakic returned as the president of the Prijedor Municipality, do you know who was the chief of police in Prijedor at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I do. The late Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recall, I'm sure, that Mr. Drljaca was -- attempted to be arrested. There was shooting. He shot an officer, and he was shot and killed in 1997. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question, Your Honour. There has been no testimony regarding the specific events relating to Mr. Drljaca's attempted arrest and ultimate shooting. I'm not sure if he shot an officer or what. I just don't want it to go in the record. If counsel wants to categorise that, he should establish if those were facts that were undisputed or not. I personally don't have any view on it, but I would hate to have any incorrections be placed on the record or any impressions to be suggested that there was a shooting of an officer. I truly don't know if there was or not. But counsel should substantiate that if he has it, and put it to the witness in that specific form as opposed to in a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Questions are how I put things, information to, witnesses. But I believe this is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a widely known fact that when Mr. Drljaca was attempted -- excuse me. When the SFOR - and I'm not sure if it was called SFOR at that time, it might have been IFOR - attempted to arrest Mr. Drljaca, that he shot a British officer, and that he was shot and killed. It was widely reported and it was a well-known fact in Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it that you don't know? You don't know that Mr. Drljaca was killed?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, I know that he was killed, but I don't know who did what. I was not present there. I didn't see it happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Mr. Drljaca -- after the attempted arrest of Mr. Drljaca, what happened to Dr. Stakic? Did he continue to make public appearances in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, don't you know that Dr. Stakic disappeared, even though he was the president of the municipality? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know that he disappeared, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I draw the attention to the fact that also answering a question with "I don't know," even though you know it would be a false answer. So please try to concentrate and try to answer a question. And we have a long line of questions you're answering just by "I don't know." And there are good reasons to believe that from the perspective of a neutral spectator of the events, you must have known. Please continue, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you consider a person calling Bosnian Muslims an artificial race to be a discriminatory statement?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, if that's true, then yes. Then it would be a discriminatory statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How did you learn about the takeover the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: When I came to work at the Prijedor Hotel, they told me that there had been a takeover last night. And I noticed a Serbian flag outside the hotel hoisted up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know who hoisted up this flag?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only make assumptions. I don't know whether you want to hear that answer. I heard that it was the soldiers who had been on security duty in front of the hotel, this mixed group of military and civilian police officers. This is what they told me at the reception desk, the receptionist on duty told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You speak about a mixed group of military and civilian police officers. Can you go in some more detail? Did you, when coming to the hotel, see such a group, mixed group of military and civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Only military police and civilian police, they were there. Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Will you please tell me, what are [inaudible] if so, did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which kind of uniform, please?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: These police officers had normal police uniforms, and these other had military police uniforms with white belts. And they had the old police insignia. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were there also people in camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to the flag hoisted up outside your hotel. Was it also the following days, weeks, and months hoisted up outside your hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: There had been a Yugoslav flag before, and then this one came. It remained there until the attack on Prijedor when it was burnt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was this hoisted up daily?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And was there anybody who ordered you or anybody else in the hotel to do so, instead of having the old flag?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The flag was hoisted on a mast, on a flag pole there, and I didn't touch it. It just remained there. It was normal for flags to be hoisted outside buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So there's no such custom that you never should have a flag hoisted up during nighttime?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you agreed, and you didn't object, to this fact that there was a flag?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Not that I didn't inquire. I was told, well, this is -- that's the way things are. Just keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We all understand that the 30th of May was a very important day in your life, and no doubt it's only by nature that you concentrate on these remarkable days in our lives. You mentioned that you recall that you heard at that date Zagreb Radio, opposed to Prijedor Radio. Did you listen the 13th --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't think that Prijedor radio was working on that day. I don't think it was. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the 13th of April? Did you listen that day, or by chance anybody else in your hotel had the radio on? Did you listen to Radio Prijedor the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
