utterances.text: No, I didn't. I couldn't tell you anything about others. There are no loud speakers for the Prijedor radio. There is no direct coverage of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the transcript, the 13th has to be exchanged against 30th April. 3-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, perhaps the witness perhaps had the translation the 13th as well, as opposed the 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I want to come back to this. Maybe there was a mistake from my side that I wasn't clear enough in my English. So we discuss the day of the takeover. Did you listen to Radio Prijedor? Weren't you interested what was said officially what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know if you will believe me, but I didn't. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: An interested member of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue. I only read from the transcript "an interested member of the party." Could you please be so kind to restate the entire sentence you wanted to present. Once again, wouldn't you yourself find it surprising that when in your hometown, a takeover takes place, that you don't try to go to find out what has happened, who is responsible, who took over, for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Again, I think it's a politician's business. They should take care of that, the party that is in power. I don't know what that was, if it was a putsch or a coup or something else. I really don't know. I really wasn't interested in all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But wouldn't this event have an impact on your own business? Isn't this reason enough to be interested in the events?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Initially, no. It did not affect the structure of the companies in terms of personnel and members of the SDS and so on and so forth. It only affected the overall situation later on, in August, September, after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When asked by Mr. Ostojic, you gave us on page 24, lines 19 following -- a short description on how you learned Dr. Stakic to know. And how was it possible for you to learn that he was a doctor from Omarska and that it was there where he completed elementary school? Did you have already at that time in the youth contact with Dr. Stakic, or did you discuss this with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, not in my youth, I didn't have any contacts with him in my youth. The first real contact came when he was appointed vice-president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For this, I thought you were not interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it just coincident that at that time when he was appointed vice-president that you had the first real contact with him in your capacity as businessman or ...?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: In my capacity as a businessman, and he, in his capacity as the vice-president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us what you discussed during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: It was a meeting of businessmen and the authorities. We usually discussed the economy, employment, the employment rate of the Prijedor Hotel, how many employees we had, and what needed to be enhanced and how we can satisfy as many clients as possible when they came to our hotel. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us earlier this morning that you learned that he was a physician in Omarska and he went to school there. Did you discuss with him the reason why he entered into the political area and, yes, became vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But at what point in time did you discuss with him his education and his development as a physician as you told us this morning?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This morning, you told us, and I just quoted from this, that when asked "you're aware that Dr. Stakic went to school in Omarska, became a physician in Omarska," when did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I learned when he came to work there as a doctor, when the young Dr. Stakic, a man from our town, came to work at the health station in Omarska. I learned this from my wife, because she was born the same year as he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been in Omarska and in the health station in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I just wasn't there when he was there. But other than that, I have been there countless times because I was born in that same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic your physician as well?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to continue a little bit. After this first meeting, when did you meet him again?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: In the period before the 30th of April, maybe two or three times, if I remember right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And after the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Then, there came a period until September during which we didn't meet. Until September 1992, I'm talking about the period between April and September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How come that just during this period you didn't have this contact apparently necessary for your business?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't think it was really necessary, had it been necessary, we would have been meeting. The hotel had been damaged, so we tried to repair the damage to our catering establishment, and Mr. Stakic must have been busy with other duties and responsibilities. Throughout that period, the hotel was not receiving guests. There may have been another meeting; I'm not sure if in September or some other month, when Dr. Stakic called me to ask me if we could host a session of the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that's what it was called at that moment. So that was my first meeting with him after the period that I talked about, since the 30th of May. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did your hotel host this session?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did. Our hotel was the venue for that meeting, I think in October that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was the leader of this meeting? Who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: It was the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina presided over by Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you participate in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was the organiser. I was the manager of the hotel. I was in charge of the technical aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall other persons by name participating in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I remember all the politicians from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time everyone attended the assembly. A colleague of mine, Branko Djeric, had just resigned. He was my generation, and he was the vice-president of the government but then he resigned. I know that a group, there was a group who tried to push for the removal of the government in Prijedor. There was Radovan Karadzic. I'm talking about the big name now. And there was Velibor Ostojic. I recognised these people, but I didn't really talk to them or have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us that you were contacted by Dr. Stakic, that Dr. Stakic called you and asked if you could host a session of the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did Dr. Stakic himself participate in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That he convened a meeting, and then there was the meeting, and I was in charge of the organisation. And then there was a meeting including a bigger group of people, and I couldn't organise this on my own, nor could he have organised this on his own. There were lots of things to be done. The glass surfaces that had been shattered had to be mended. Everything had to be prepared. There were lots of things to be sorted out. The big hall to hold the assembly, with no water, no electricity. That's what it was like back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you during this phone call already confirm this meeting that your hotel would be ready to host this group, or did you have a follow-up meeting with Dr. Stakic to discuss details of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic told me then that I should give it some thought, and then there was another meeting during which we discussed the details of the whole thing. But not only the two of us, there was a group of people involved. And then tasks were handed out. There was a second meeting, and then a third meeting. There were a number of meetings concerning the organising of this assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when concretely took this meeting place in your hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The exact date, I think it was on the 23rd of October, 1992, the 22nd or the 23rd. It lasted for three days. I'm not sure if it was October or November. It was late in 1992. I know that an electricity aggregate had to be supplied because we had no water, electricity, or heating. And it was very cold in the rooms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then later on, you told us that Dr. Stakic came several times to your hotel. This is correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, the vice-president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, the secretary for the economy, everyone came. It lasted for about a month, the preparations of the assembly. Day in, day out. The late Simo Drljaca, he practically spent most of his time at the hotel because he was in charge of security, sabotage work, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But must have had in-depth discussion with Dr. Stakic that you are able to come to the assessment that Dr. Stakic was, as it was the assessment of a number of witnesses we heard here, a moderate person. What brought you to this conclusion, on what basis was this? Did you have special good contacts with Dr. Stakic? Did you discuss, and I still try to find out, how did you learn -- this was the beginning of the line of questions. How did you learn about issues? Did you discuss this with him, and did you discuss with him the question whether or why he entered into the political area and then later no longer, for a period of time, acted as president of the Municipal Assembly, all these issues, what one would normally discuss when being in a closer contact?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, yes. But this is the sort of conversation that you usually leave for more peaceful times. Those times in Prijedor were terrible, not only for Prijedor but also for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had no time and no room left for intimate conversations, debating all these issues. Whenever I talked to him, I always got the impression that first and foremost, he was a doctor to begin with. And then after that, perhaps also a politician. His role in organising the assembly was also to organise, to hand out specific tasks to the different members of the committee so these tasks could be carried out. I did not have much direct personal contact with him. I was handed out my task, and then another person was handed out theirs, you know, that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. But may I ask you, to the best of your recollection, what were the functions of Dr. Stakic? You mentioned already his role as vice-president. And then were there, in addition, other functions?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: As the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, I'm not sure if he headed any committee or any of the bodies. I don't know that. But I know that after he was removed, he returned to work as the chief of the health centre, the head of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where was he removed? I quote from your answer: "After he was removed ..."

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand you perfectly. From the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, that was -- the removal was in January 1993 as far as I can remember. But I know that from September 1992, the SDS people wanted already to remove Dr. Stakic from his position, and then finally they succeeded. Their president at that time, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, I knew they had a meeting of the main board at the Prijedor Hotel. And at that meeting they said that things would remain as they were until the beginning of 1993. And then at what I thought was the first meeting of the main board of the SDS in January 1993, Mr. Stakic was removed. And then Dusan Kurnoga became the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What were the reasons, to the best of your recollection, that from "from September 1992, the SDS people wanted already to remove Dr. Stakic from his position"?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I realised, and it was my conviction, that he was not sufficiently radical. He was not sufficiently, if I may say, aggressive. He was no hawk. He belonged to the moderate faction inside the party. He believed in reason, in understanding, in tolerance. And then people came along who, you know, had different ideas about how to go about certain things. They wanted things done differently. That was my understanding because I can't possibly see what the reason would have been for them otherwise to request his removal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic a member of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was his function in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I never attended any of their meetings. And I never read their book of rules or their programme, so I'm not familiar with that. I can't answer the question. The only thing I can say is I don't know. Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been in the building of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you visit Dr. Stakic in this building?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where was his office located?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: His office was on the second floor. The vice-president's office was to the right, and the president's office was to the left as you walked past the secretaries' room. That's the first floor, excuse me. First comes the ground floor, and then you climb on to the first floor. That's where the office was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What did you discuss with him in this building?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Again, it was a meeting of a number of businessmen. I may have been a bit early, so I came in, I greeted him, hello, how are you doing. We used to have this everyday kind of conversation. We talked about the hotel. We needed money to repair the remaining damage, the entrance hall, the first floor, the reception and a number of rooms on the upper floored that been destroyed completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it only once or several times you visited him there?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: During that period, I can only remember this single case. That's while he was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was what? Your sentence was not complete. "That's while he was..."?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: President, during his first term of office, the president of the Municipal Assembly, during the first term of office. And after this assembly was held, during that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, to be more concrete, which month approximately?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, let's say the end of December, when data was gathered and presented, data about companies and how successful the companies were. The annual budget is drawn up, and then plans are made for the following year, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's go back to the end of May. On page 34, line 11, you were asked by the Prosecution: "Were you aware that -- isn't it true that after that day, and the next couple of days, people were told to go to your hotel, non-Serbs, where they were transported from there to camps such as Omarska?" And then you answer: "No, I don't think that's true." Only to avoid any kind of ambiguity, because in fact there were two questions in one, is it true that people were brought or persons were brought to your hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I've referred to this in my testimony, yes. People did come, but only to spend a single night. This gentleman, I can't remember his name, I didn't exactly know him very well. He had brought a large group of people from Kozarac, Kozarusa, and the other villages, to put them up at the Prijedor Hotel for the night. And that was done. And what happened later, where they were taken, I really don't know. I've said this already to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the ethnicity of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I suppose Muslims. I assume most of them were Muslims, because they were the population in that region. The population in that area was mostly Muslim, and there were some Croats living there, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How did they leave your hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, they had breakfast at the hotel, and then they just simply left. They had a man who was in charge, who organised everything. It was not like the Red Cross, you know. Someone just came up as a self-appointed leader of the group who took charge of the group. He was middle-aged, quite lean. I can't really remember the man well. There was another such case in the autumn of 1991 when Kostujnica in Croatia had fallen, and the same thing happened. A large group of people came from Bosanska Kostujnica, reached the Prijedor Hotel, spent the night there, and then on the following day they all went back to their houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to the end of May, beginning the June. These people in your hotel, when they left, they left together? They left by bus? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, certainly not by bus. They left individually, or in groups. Friends and relatives would come from the town, so there were certainly no buses outside the hotel waiting to take them away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it from your testimony, they -- all of them entered voluntarily your hotel and left the hotel voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Voluntary. I don't know why they would left their homes in the first place. But they weren't escorted by the police or the army to my hotel. And that was also how they left. They left unescorted. I'm not sure, maybe there was something else, too. There was a group of Muslims in the stadium; those were bussed there. But that had nothing to do with the hotel. That was completely unrelated, and that's on the other bank of the River Sana, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, which stadium do you refer to when saying "there was a group of Muslims in the stadium"?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The stadium, we call it Suhi Prijedor. It's a football pitch that's being constructed for the Rudar football club. There are sports grounds being constructed there. It's on the left bank of the River Sana, general direction of Hambarine and Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They were just Muslims, and who do you believe is responsible for this, call it, "special treatment" of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I believe the national parties were responsible, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I leave you with this answer. Before the break, just one short question. You mentioned a checkpoint at the bridge. This checkpoint, or maybe there were even several checkpoints, were manned by whom?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Police. Civilian police, the reserve forces, and the active-duty forces. Policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From Prijedor, or from outside?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from Prijedor. As far as I could tell, they were from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was the period in time you had to cross these checkpoints? When were they established, and when were they deleted?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well -- well, they were set up in mid-May, I think, and then they were dismantled sometime probably before the assembly I talked about. But I'm not sure about the time period. I really can't specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand it's ten years ago. But only to conclude this, probably before the assembly? What do you mean by "before the assembly"?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I mean, they were abolished prior to the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the one we've already talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to this later after the break. The trial stays adjourned until 12.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Kos, we briefly touched upon the issue of persons you called extremists. Did they wear any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand your question. In which time period? What uniforms? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the attack on Prijedor or during the attack on Prijedor, the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they wore uniforms. The JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That there is no misunderstanding, the persons -- I asked whether or not the persons you called extremists, did they wear any kind of uniform at that time, end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, they wore military uniforms during the attack. But I couldn't see what kind of insignia they had. But the colour of the uniform was olive grey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which army took part in this fighting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: In this fighting? Well, at the beginning, it was the police. Afterwards, the regular and mobilised soldiers joined in. I don't know whose army it was, the JNA of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know how it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you don't have anything more about details?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which capacity did you know him? He acted -- to be more concrete, he acted in which capacity in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Srdic was the president of the SDS party and a deputy in the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall anything related to, first, 30th of May, 1992; and second, Mr. Srdjo Srdic? Was there anything special that happened to this person?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember that his apartment was broken in, but I don't know when that happened. Maybe you are referring to his house, which was built -- which was, sorry, destroyed on that day. There was a cafe which was part of this house called MD. That's what I saw when I came back to Prijedor on the first day. I don't know when it was destroyed, whether in the actual fighting or later. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was destroyed the entire house or the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The cafe. There were other buildings that were destroyed there as well. The cafe was destroyed. I know about that. But you know, it's a row of houses. I don't know exactly where his house begins and where it ends. I didn't observe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally. While I was a manager with the Namteks company, he used to work there as a maintenance worker. He repaired refrigerators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, was there something special happening to Mr. Zoran Karlica on or about the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: According to what I know, it happened on the 30th of May. He was severely wounded near a house where there was a cafe called Obala, from where they shot at the Prijedor Hotel and JNA Street and Partizanska Street as well, these two streets. I think he tried to climb the stairs and was severely wounded on that occasion. He was transferred first to Banja Luka and from there to Belgrade where he succumbed to his injuries which were caused, I believe, by a hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know personally or from that what you learned from Mr. Karlica who threw this hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know that personally. It's -- this is just what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What did you hear? Who was --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether it was Slavko Ecimovic or someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's leave it with this, in the light of the proffer we got from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Again, this is something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What did you hear about camps in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: What I heard, I heard -- well, according to the information I got, those were more like collection centres, so to speak, for purposes of moving the population to their desired destinations. There were people who wanted to go to Zagreb, others who wanted to go to Sarajevo. And it was for that purpose that they were established. But I couldn't tell you when exactly they were opened up. The Keraterm camp is the one that is closest to my house. I noticed that one, not others, until this group of international journalists arrived and made it all public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You just stated that the Keraterm camp, that is the one closest to your house. What did you observe there? What changed before the takeover and after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Initially, during the first month, nothing really changed so far as I could observe. I didn't actually go passed this building because it is located on the Prijedor/Banja Luka/Novi Grad communication, because at the time, I didn't have a car so I couldn't travel along that road. I went to work by bicycle along a less busy road. But yes, to be frank, I did pass by a couple of occasions, and I noticed some people there. The building is located some 300 metres away from the road. And before the war, I used to go to this factory. It was a small factory of -- which produced fire-proof material. It was part of a larger combine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, when it was no longer used for this purpose at that time, what happened? What was changed?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, what happened was -- I don't know the exact date, but I know, for instance, that the manager of the factory lived in the hotel until the breakout of the conflict on the 30th of May. He was from Zenica by origin, and this factory was part of a larger factory there. So they had common human resources policy. Some of the people were appointed from Zenica and some others from Prijedor by the Zenica municipal authorities, that is. Then these journalists came, and this is when I heard that there was a camp, as you say, what we used to call it a collection centre. There were guards there, and I heard that there had been a major incident one night. It was on the following day that I learned that this -- I don't know what to call it, rebellion, disorder, had occurred. A number of people got killed. Fire was opened, and there were stories according to which apparently a group of drunken youths had caused it. Apparently a group of people -- now, I'm telling you only what I heard from others. Some sort of extremists apparently got there. They rebelled. They attacked the guard post, wanted to go home. This is all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us that the manager of this factory was accommodated in your hotel for a certain period of time. Did he tell you why he couldn't continue with the production of the goods as it was before?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, we never talked about that during that time period. But then again, we didn't talk very often to each other. He only stayed there overnight. He slept there, and we didn't meet very frequently. As for that period of time, 30th of April onwards, I really saw him very rarely. People didn't meet often in those days, businessmen, politicians. And I didn't see him during that time period, so I was not able to learn anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see, yourself, persons in this area detained?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I did. Once or maybe two times, when somebody would give me a lift, I saw it. During the day, either going to work or coming home from work, I saw that there was a large group of people outside the factory, outside the buildings which were part of the factory. I couldn't see clearly because the distance after all is 300, 350 metres. I couldn't see much of them. I couldn't recognise any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know the reason why these persons were detained there?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I think, from what I know, and I don't know whether this is the truth or -- not, there had apparently been some lists of members of the party, lists of persons who wanted a different outcome of the war, and were somehow related with events that took place in Prijedor town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who do you think is responsible for this detention?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Who's responsible. You know, what was characteristic about Prijedor was that there were three parties. Then there was the civilian -- there were civilian authorities, military authorities, police authorities. They all wanted to be autonomous, independent. And it was really hard to tell for anyone who was issuing orders, who was taking orders, who was subordinate to whom. And at that time, as far as the camps were concerned, mostly the military would take people to the camp, and then the whole thing would be taken over by the police. But who issued orders to whom, I don't know. I know that the security of the camps was provided by the police, or more precisely, if you want me to say, Mr. Simo Drljaca. And I'm very sorry that I have to say bad things about a dead person. But I think that that's as close to the truth as it gets. But again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you give us other names of camps or, you call it, collection centres in Prijedor Municipality you are aware of in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I became aware of that in late August. I learned about the Omarska and Trnopolje camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in comparison to this, what about the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't understand which football stadium you're referring to. The only one was located in Trnopolje, next to the school building. I am familiar with the area relatively well. I don't know Omarska. I mean, I was -- I've never actually been to Trnopolje itself, but I know the area. I even visited the school once with my friends. But before the war, not during this period of time. But if you're referring to the stadium in Tukovi, that was before. There was a small group of people. Apparently something was going on in the area of Brdo, in this hilly area. And I got a call from a friend, from a waiter - I don't remember what his name was - that children should be put up there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we didn't get the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then the next day, everybody left the stadium. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The interpretation didn't get the last part of your answer. You started, "and I got a call from a friend, from a waiter - I don't remember what his name was - that children should be put up there." This I can read from the transcript. Apparently there seems to be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Okay, I will repeat. There was a large group of men, women, and children at that stadium, including a waiter who worked in my establishment. He called me that some of us should come to where he was take the children to the town to stay with some of their friends. Since I did not have a car, I asked Slavko Davidovic, the then manager of the hotel, who then took me there. And he took the children to these friends. But I don't know who they are. But this waiter is from Hambarine. I know that the next day, he called. He was somewhere where the buses were, and apparently he was leaving. I don't know exactly where he left, but he left with his wife and children. I'm not sure where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which buses, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: It was on the following day, I believe all of the buses belonged to the Autotransport bus company. I never saw those buses. This is just what I heard from other people. But it is possible that some also belonged to the mine company, because they had their own pool of buses. But I didn't see that. That's what people told. I know that there were buses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, did you see ever paramilitary groups in Prijedor? And if yes, on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I did see groups of people. I don't know if they were paramilitary or not. There was this Janjceva group, Milica group. Well, Zoran Karlica's group was somewhat different than the rest. Then there was a group apparently that had arrived from Serbia and from another town such as Bjeljina, for instance. But I personally never saw them. I saw Janjceva group, the one that was led by the late Janic whom I used to know. But it was not a paramilitary group. It was under the command of our guys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry if I ask, when you say "our guys," what do you mean by this? "It was under the" --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, when I said "our," I was referring to the regular army which was part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and which was under their command. It was a slip when I said that they were "our guys."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, you told us that at the end of 1991, beginning 1992, Muslims started to leave Prijedor while Serbs were sending away their children and wives. Why it happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I didn't say Serbs. I said some Serbs, a number of Serbs. I'm not sure how it was translated. But it was due to the tension which had arisen because of the war in Croatia, because the borders were there. Those were two neighbouring republics. And someone seemed to have wanted this war in that area. Someone seemed to see it coming. And some people didn't believe. I stayed behind with my family. I have two daughters. I never thought of going away. I just told myself, just wait and see what happens. Fear of a new war or of some people's ambitions, I'm not sure if those ambitions could actually come to fruition ever. I don't know, but that's how I felt. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You also said at page 10 of the transcript, line 25: "There was a certain amount of fear with non-Serb population." Again, what kind of fear?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: It wasn't only the non-Serb population. Everyone felt fear, the whole population. It's only that the non-Serb population wanted more badly to leave that area so that they could -- well, I don't know, perhaps return. I know that men mostly did return later on. I know this from places in my own company, and they would send their children away, abroad, most often. They were waiting, biding their time, to see what would happen. No one really spoke out loud in favour of the war, but you could feel it in the air because you had those nationalistic parties, they were stoking up the fire with their public statements. They said "war is better than a rotten peace." And then the war in Croatia was inevitable. There had been a truce signed already at that point, but there were a lot of soldiers involved, JNA soldiers, blameless soldiers, who simply got killed there. In Slovenia or in Croatia, they were just doing their regular military service there, and they were just caught up in the middle of this, were killed, and never returned home. That's about it. That's as far as I can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You told us that the attackers of Prijedor on 30th of May, 1992, retreated through Stari Grad. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I believe that to be correct. I didn't see them myself. But by all accounts, yes, that's where they passed through, because that's where they had come from. One group came from there, and there was another group which had arrived from Puharska. I never said that I personally witnessed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And how much time it took for them to retreat through Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, the centre itself does not cover a very large area. It all depends on where exactly they were passing through. I can't say. Half an hour perhaps, an hour, two hours. It's impossible for me to tell. I know that my present friend was seriously wounded on the bridge, and he hid in the shrubbery there, Mr. Marijan Nisic. And he was captured later on, and he was the one who told me the story at a later stage. But I didn't personally witness this, I'm just bringing you the eyewitness accounts of what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you think that it was possible to destroy Stari Grad in half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. By no means. Can't be done. I'm not sure what I mean by "destroy." No, I don't think it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned that by chance, you observed a meeting or a rally of supporters of national radical party headed by lawyer Guberina. Correct? When it was happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't by accident. The only coincidence was that I was on my way to see my relatives there, and once there I found that this pre-election meeting was taking place. But it was simply something I found along the way. I'm not sure what sort of coincidence that is. But that's the village of Nisevici. Kanovic is the maiden name of my wife, so I was going there to see my relatives. So call it a coincidence if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: When it happened, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The elections were taking place from summer to autumn. I really can't remember now. Milica Gaj, I know the forest there, I know all of that but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: In autumn of 1990. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, or perhaps 1989. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Before that time, have you heard about lawyer Guberina and about his party?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I had heard of him. But I don't think I'd ever heard of his party or that he was about to found a party. I told you I read the Politika newspapers, and I read about Guberina and about those lawyers over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And at this meeting or rally, what was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't really stay for too long. It was a promotional campaign for the foundation of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And who participated in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Veljko Guberina spoke on and on for hours, so I just got bored stiff and I left at a certain point. He can talk the hind legs off a donkey. He's really that kind of man. Once he starts speaking, there's no stopping him. There were many people on the stage there, so you know I couldn't tell them apart. I was just bored to death. That's the truth of it. You know, there were five or six of them up there on the stage lined up, and he was also standing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the role of Dr. Stakic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Not that I could provide any details. I don't know. He was just standing there, and Mr. Stakic took part, was a member of the organisational committee for the setting up of the party in the Prijedor area. But I don't know. I didn't stay there for long. I know that he was there. I know that Veljko was there. And I know that the party operated for a while, but then I heard -- but when exactly this was, I really don't know. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And before that meeting, did you know Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No. I'd only heard of him. I heard that he started working in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: After university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just add before passing the floor, how come that you identified Mr. Stakic at that meeting when you haven't met him before?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, my brother-in-law, my wife's brother, he said: "There, you see Stakic is over there." He pointed his finger at him. So he was to have one of the leading positions, he said. But his hair was sort of thinning like mine, so that's when I saw him. That's when he was pointed out to me. Usually when people are standing over there on that stage, you ask yourself questions about who's going to be what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But Dr. Stakic did not take the floor and addressed people at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I really don't know. I told you my story. Guberina talked on for hours and hours on end. I just got bored and I left; I split at one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understood. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I have something like a curiosity. On page 66, line 2 of the transcript, you were talking about paramilitary groups. You said that there were groups coming from other parts of the country, and you talk about the Janic or something like that. And please, I apologise for the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that Zoran Karlica's group, that's the translation, was somewhat different than the rest. May I ask you how was this group different?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, it was not a paramilitary unit to begin with. It was part of the army, and it was subordinate to the military command. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I thought you meant that for the other group.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. I was only referring to this group. They were called the reconnoitering group of Major Zoran Karlica, and there were other paramilitary groups. There were usually groups, paramilitary groups, military units set up with a number of people that someone would be appointed their leader, and then that person would say, okay, I'm the head of this group. But no one had any idea of who was in control or in command. The police or the army. You couldn't know for certain. Someone had to be in charge but I couldn't really tell you who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Is this Mr. Karlica the same man who sustained injuries on the 30th of May in the attack to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the very same man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a different question. I'm moving to another side. You've done your military service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's correct. In the JNA in 1977 in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Then you know something about the structures of the army, because I have not made military service because I am a woman and in my country women are not supposed to do those sort of things. May I ask you, how many men composed a battalion?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: A battalion should normally have a 1.500 up to 2.000 men, but that really depends on the structure. Two, three squads I think, or more -- correction companies two or three companies or more. I may have been wrong. Excuse me, I was talking about the brigade. This is smaller. This is up to 500 people. So a correction there. A battalion should normally comprise three companies, and the brigade should number between 1.500 and 2.000 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know that there were army barracks in Prijedor in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did you know which brigade was set there?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: It was the Yugoslav, I think, 143rd, now called the 43rd. I can't tell you the date exactly, but there was a brigade stationed there. 343rd, 43rd, 143rd, I'm not sure what it's called today, but there was a brigade that was set up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. And was it a motorised brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, motorised, infantry and motorised. I think that's also what it was called, infantry motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And this brigade had tanks?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did. A battalion of tanks, and the military, the artillery, all sorts of things. I think it was part of -- I can't give you the precise structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence has any further -- do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please feel free. It's your testimony, if you want to add something spontaneously, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, Your Honours. This has been a very pleasant experience for me. I tried to give you my truth. Now how much that truth is worth, it is up to you to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. There's no one truth, and we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I think, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- From all sides, and therefore we have to hear all the sides and all participants and this indeed enlightens us. May I ask the Defence, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just a few points I'd like you to clarify, sir. Further cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you ever discuss politics with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm saying this expressly and unequivocally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with him issues like the camps in Prijedor or the removal of the non-Serb population from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Same answer, unequivocally, no. These were, these were thorny issues, so I didn't really discuss them with anyone, including Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, when you told us that Dr. Stakic was not a hawk, you've already told us you never heard any of his speeches, and you told us you never privately discussed politics with him. So really, you don't know what his position was on the issues of the policies in Prijedor in 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour, and it's obviously in my opinion taken out of context. When the Court asked the question, I believe it was relating to the meeting that occurred subsequent to the time period of the indictment and the reasons why people were seeking to remove Dr. Stakic, and the witness answered the Court directly on that. And I think quite frankly, with all due respect to my learned friend, it is a bit out of context to put the question to him like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After deliberation, dismissed for that that is evident, that the question summarises that what was said by the witness. And it's just a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said, the opinion of the SDS members was that there should be a hawk in Dr. Stakic's place. I'm not sure how this was translated. But that what they meant to say was someone more extremist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not present during this meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't. I wasn't sitting with them, but they did have these meetings quite frequently in my hotel. And on their way into the hall, they would have conversations, you know, we'll remove this man, we'll put another one in his place. He's not hard line enough for us. He doesn't have the penetrating force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear that there were allegations that humanitarian aid in Prijedor was being misused or that there was corruption in humanitarian aid during the presidency of Dr. Stakic, and that's why he was removed?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: The first part of your question, yes, I heard that. But whether that was the reason, I don't think that could have been the reason because the Red Cross was undisputed there, as well as Mr. Srdjo Srdic. They had people coming and checking on them, and no misuse of funds was ever established. So I don't think that was the reason because the Red Cross was in charge and fully in charge of humanitarian aid, and you know that the Red Cross was headed by Srdjo Srdic. He was totally in charge; that's certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, another quick question: You were talking about people leaving Prijedor prior to the takeover of the municipality. Is it also true that often young men left Prijedor for Belgrade in order to avoid military service? Was that a phenomenon that was well known?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: In order to avoid military service, or mobilisation callup, can you please clarify a little. Did you mean the regular military service, or did you mean just them being mobilised? I'm not sure which one you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm referring to is people, and particularly in this case, I'm asking you about Serb young men. I understand it took place among other nationalities also. That young Serbian men --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in order to -- okay. I think we understand each other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Yes, that's right. There were Serbs, not only non-Serbs, but also Serbs who were fit for military service but dodged military service and left for Serbia or for another country. And less probably than in other places, but now, even, they are returning. They are coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the meeting that you attended in Dr. Stakic's office, just, first, I just want to clarify something about the physical layout of the office. Is it correct that when you first enter, you enter into the area that the secretary sits? And on one side is the office of the president of the municipality; and on the other side is the office of the vice-president, that both of them you enter, first going through the secretarial area?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: One of the secretaries, yes, yes, that's correct. The vice-president and the president have their own secretaries each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, how many --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Correction, the same secretary does work for both the president and the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, how many businessmen were attendance, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, five or six. Not too many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of those businessmen Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was your house from the Keraterm facility?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: About 3 kilometres, I would say. It's still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall one night late in July hearing gunfire for a very long time that evening, sustained gunfire?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of gunfire, but that was not unusual. The military would come back from the front line, and they would just start shooting. You didn't know who was shooting, those returning from their shift, because every 45 days, you had new soldiers being sent to the front and old soldiers coming back. Whether the shooting, the gunfire, was coming from Keraterm, I can't know that for sure because I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you heard about what you called the incident at Keraterm, and if you do not object, I'm going to use the word "massacre." You heard about the massacre at Keraterm the day after it happened. Isn't it true that a lot of people were talking about that in Prijedor, and that many people had heard the gunfire during the night?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: That's true, but no one really knew what was actually happening. The truth has a habit of emerging usually quite late. And compared to those standards, this was quite fast. Sometimes it takes years and decades. Serbs were afraid, too. There was fear among the Serbian population. People were concerned. They had genuine concern for their women, for their elderly, for the children. No one was exactly excited about what was happening or what happened on that day. You heard about people getting killed on the front or even members of different informal groups coming in and out of the camps, innocent people, blameless people. But that was the reality of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that what you had heard is that it was committed by a group of young drunks, and I think you also at one time used the word "extremists" who the police guards were unable to control. None of those individuals were ever arrested as far as you know. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: I don't know about those. I know about the guards, the guards were all arrested and they were all brought to justice, to answer for their omissions and what their omissions were exactly, I'd best just leave it to up to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But just to be clear that we understand what you're talking about, you're talking about the guards being arrested by the Tribunal. Is that correct? By this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never --

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: And they answered for not having prevented those hoards, drunken hoards, or whoever they were, from doing whatever they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think as you said, history will judge that. Sir, are you aware of any investigation or any arrests in Prijedor, by the Prijedor authorities, of the persons that perpetrated that massacre?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, are you aware of any actions or attempts at action by Dr. Stakic to prevent or punish crimes that happened in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO KOS
utterances.text: Not that I know of, any attempts. That period, 1992, you know, the second period, it just came like that. No, not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No further questions. And it remains for me to thank you, not only for coming but also for testifying before this Tribunal. As you yourself stated, it's important to hear both sides and all sides of the truth. And it assisted us in this attempt. We wish you good and safe trip home. Thank you. You are excused for today. And may the usher please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence wanted to raise three issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We had a couple issues, if we may discuss. The first one is that I was able to visit with Mr. Makovski last night briefly, and he informed me that he was not given access and was not given the opportunity to visit with Dr. Stakic. And he wanted me to raise it with the Court if I may. And Dr. Stakic has informed me of the same. So I just wanted the record to reflect that although we requested and felt that the Court granted our request, it has been denied and it has not occurred, much to our disappointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm taken by surprise on this, and my apologies to Dr. Stakic, because we indeed agreed and granted this visit. I don't know what the reason is. We have to come back to this. Please, next issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The second issue relates to certain disclosures that we received a while back that has been the subject of some discussion here this week. The OTP provided us with transcripts of initially five, and I believe six, statements taken from various individuals. We subsequent to that had requested, because they were transcripts which were done in English, we requested that the tapes being provided to us. It's my understanding that the position of the OTP is that they agreed to that. Ms. Joanna Korner last Friday when I met with her provided me with six tapes. Upon reviewing and copying the tapes, so that we could share it and give it to your client, we find that the tapes that were given to us were of only one individual. And that individual did, indeed, through his interview, I think there were six changes in his tape. So we would like to formally to request, with the Court's assistance, the remaining tapes of those individuals so that our client with participate and assist us on issues that we believe have been raised from those transcripts and that production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could work this out between ourselves and counsel. That was my understanding of the original immediate request was for the tapes of that one individual, because we thought that was what was necessary at the time. The remaining ones we can review. There is just one issue, and that is these individuals who were summoned and were interviewed did not give their consent. They were asked information, for example, about their home address and families and they did not consent to that to be disclosed. So I don't know how we're going to deal with that as far as Dr. Stakic. But I'm sure we can work it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can inform the OTP that the transcripts clearly reflect their home address and telephone number. To the extent there's any concern, and I don't believe that there should be, if we can redact it, there would be no objection from the Defence on that. But just to remember, we do have the transcripts with that information fully disclosed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Right. And that's provided to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this matter can be resolved, no doubt, that Dr. Stakic has a right to listen to these tapes in a language he understands. Otherwise, the statements would have to be translated. But I've no doubt that this will be cured immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think I have a suggestion. We can discuss it privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope this will be resolved. Next issue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just final issue also involves Rule 68 disclosure. We were given on I believe two separate filings initially nine witness statement summaries, and subsequent to that, 21 witness summaries. We had requested in our motion which was respectfully denied, that in the alternative, those witness statements in their whole be produced to us. And I understood that they would be, but we have not received them to date. What we did receive on those disclosures was specifically a one- to three-line summation of the testimony within those witness statements. The Defence would like the opportunity to view the witness statements in its entirety. And obviously don't object to having any redaction done on any sensitive information. The purpose for this is because we would like to compare those witness statements with the testimony that was proffered during the Prosecutor's case in chief, and to determine what, for example, the inconsistencies may have been and how any of the statements as a whole can be viewed as being exculpatory to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We would be happy to provide those. There may be a mix up. I didn't understand that the Defence wanted those. But -- and there is just a procedure where we do have to go through and redact them. It is also possible that someone else did understand and that process is under way. But it does take a little bit of time and I'll make sure that it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. That's all we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not at this time, and I don't think I need to tell the Court that we still have an issue with the summaries, and particularly this witness's Rule 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact, no doubt, we have to come back to this issue immediately after the Court recess. But I want for the transcript to emphasise that apparently, at least the Judges - I don't know what about the Prosecution - do not have proffers for the following witness: First, I give you the number defined by the registry; second, the 65 ter number. This would be the following witnesses: 6/12, 10/17, 15/26, 21/38, 35/56, 45/74, 50/82, 53/85, 56/91. What I can say already today is that these proffers have to be provided carefully and thoroughly, and I was absolutely taken by surprise to hear today's witness statement. This had nothing to do with that we could find in the summary of the testimony, and the same is true when we discussed the question whether it is really necessary or relevant to hear this witness on transcript pages 9.280 to 9.282. I think the Defence will understand when comparing, for example, the second paragraph of the summary of this testimony. It is far from that what we heard today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to go into far more details. We mentioned already that the date of birth, today it was correct, has to be correct, and we have to provide it to be provided with the exact coordinates of the witness because the Trial Chamber feels obliged in the one or other case to find out ourselves what we have available on these witnesses. We mentioned already yesterday the proffer related to Witness 65 ter number 44, which, in fact, once again was far from that what we heard from this young witness. And if we would have known what the witness can testify, we would never have allowed this witness to be called. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence most certainly, with all due respect, needs clarification on the issue if the witness that we just had before us, that his testimony was not consistent with the proffer submitted under his Defence witness number 45 summation. The Defence submits, for the record, that we identified in the summary of our testimony that this witness was going to talk and to give testimony pertinent to May 30th, 1992. The Defence genuinely believes that this witness did provide testimony in connection with that date. Similarly, the Defence stated that the witness's -- the witness would testify, among other things, about people coming from the Kozara area to Prijedor for a period of time. The translation from someone who is an "izbjeglica" or someone called "bjezi" from Kozarac may have been lost by identifying these individuals as refugees from Kozarac. I think the witness clarified that issue when he testified. The witness also explained who in his view, upon his personal observation, took part in the fighting. Although the Defence doesn't think that it's pertinent which specific house was damaged in this particular time, information was provided to us that Mr. Srdjo Srdic's house was destroyed, and the witness testified consistent with that. Similarly, the Defence was provided with information that Zoran Karlica was wounded inside a house. The Defence likewise is of the position that the witness testified consistent with that. The Defence is confused. If that doesn't meet the standards, we would need to specifically, with all due respect, know what else is it other than a deposition that we should supply to the Court and to counsel on these witnesses? Just by way of brief background, I recognise that there have been some errors, and I truly believe that they were typographical errors with respect to dates on the date of birth. The sum and substance of the testimony of the witnesses that we have proffered to date I genuinely believe were consistent with that which was in the summary. The OTP has never raised the issue of surprise or prejudice, and yet called us on a couple, I believe, a couple -- at least one occasion to make verification of certain data to confirm that they have the right person despite of these typographical errors. With respect to the witness that testified, I believe, number 44, as DE, that witness, with all due respect to the Court, the Defence feels was relevant despite the fact, although the year of his birth was correct, he was 16 years old. The OTP confronted the witness because they were somewhat suspicious that his name was misspelled, despite the fact that the Defence wrote the name down and it was introduced as an exhibit. The OTP asked for his identification card. The OTP has not raised an issue that there was any inconsistency with that identification card because it is they who had it wrong and thought it was a different individual with a similar spelling. The identification card was consistent with the way we identified the individual. The Defence also believes that it is our duty, since the OTP raises issues, whether this Court ultimately deems them to be relevant or not, it is our duty to confront those issues and to bring the truth before this Tribunal. If the Defence says that it was raining and it was not, it is our obligation to bring witnesses to say that it was not. If the Defence says that children were expelled and prevented from going to schools, we felt and feel that a witness such as DF should at the time being a student, despite the fact that his town and that area was summarily dismissed pursuant to 98 bis, that he has relevant data as an eyewitness to tell us who was in the school and for what period of time. We apologise if the date of birth or the city that he came -- was from would have struck this witness, the Defence would have certainly applied to the Court to provide what I thought, quite candidly, with all due respect, was relevant data to refute and contradict some of the allegations that were raised by the OTP relating to issues starting even with the joint criminal enterprise, a plan to expel children and teachers, that everyone was discharged. Those were their statements in their opening argument. Those were their statements from their witnesses. The Defence truly believes we have an unequivocal right to rebut, contradict, and establish any inconsistencies with the evidence that they have presented. The Defence also finally would like to add for the Court, we will most certainly endeavour to provide the most accurate data to both the Court and the OTP with respect to the background information of these witnesses. We were somewhat hurried when we provided these. There were some changes when they were provided. We certainly apologise if it has caused any inconvenience to the Court, its staff, or the OTP and its staff. We will endeavour to confirm on at least two separate occasions that all that information is consistent by personally examining the identification cards of these individuals for that verification as opposed to relying on notes from what an investigator or an attorney would hear from a witness. But I would like, with the Court's permission, to be given some more guidance as to the extent of the summary. And I underscore the word pursuant to Rule 65 ter, the summary of the witness's testimony that the Court would like us to provide, and we will endeavour to do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We didn't want to have a closing argument. Maybe it's your closing argument for this year. We have to come back, no doubt, to this issue in the presence of both Defence counsel, and then we may clarify this. And I also believe when you compare the transcript of today with the transcript of the day when we admitted the evidence and tried to find out which witness to strike from the list or not, there are some discrepancies. But we all have time enough for the next period in time to read all this. I take it that for the first eight days of the working days in January, starting with the 8th of January, we have the eight witnesses on the list the Defence provided us with; and in addition, number 43, that is 65 ter number 71 on the list. And I take it that this will suffice to fill the entire time given for these eight days. In case there should be an absence or a witness should fall ill, please take it that the Trial Chamber is prepared to hear another substituting witness in this case, because we have to work due to our schedule, and we can't afford any day without hearing witnesses. This concludes not only today's hearing; this concludes also this year's hearing. This 93rd day of this case. I hope that we will be able to come as soon as possible in the framework, no doubt, of a fair trial to conclusions, conclusions based on that what you can identify on the basis of the 98 bis decision as the opinion of the Chamber, opposed to that what is referred to as, and this is no doubt the test, the conclusion to what may come a reasonable trial of fact. Both parties should be aware of the difference that makes. And the Trial Chamber will not hesitate, as soon as possible, to continue with judicial hints in order to streamline already during the first months of the upcoming year this case to the necessary and to the remaining charges and incidents. We come back to this step by step as soon as we have come to a conclusion on legal issues. Finally, and deep heartedly, I have to thank all the participants in this case for the work, for the sometimes difficult but in criminal-law cases, this is normal, sometimes difficult cooperation. But in most cases, good cooperation as far as this was possible. And I thank, first of all, the interpreters. Without your assistance, we would not be able to understand each other. And I think in a broader sense, this is the first mandate of this Tribunal, to make people understand each other. I wish you all good holidays and a good Christmas whenever it's your religion, and let's hope that we all together have a peaceful new year. Thank you.
